Basal metabolic rate in the Tui (Prosthemadera novaeseelandiae) was measured under controlled conditions using flow-through respirometry. The maximum resting metabolic rate recorded for this species reached 199 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 199 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when individuals were maintained at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a value consistent with the high energetic demands of a largely nectarivorous diet. Hatchlings emerge from the egg at an extremely small size, with neonatal wet weight averaging just 7.31 grams [Ww0 = 7.31 grams], reflecting the altricial nature of the nestling chick. This initial mass is among the lowest recorded for passerines of similar adult dimensions, necessitating rapid parental provisioning and intense brooding during the first days post-hatching. The energetic investment required to thermoregulate and stimulate feeding in such a tiny neonate likely constrains clutch size and brood success in this species, particularly during cooler breeding seasons in its New Zealand forest habitat.

Incubation temperature plays a critical role in determining the onset of hatching in the Tui. Under laboratory conditions where eggs were held at a constant temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], the age at birth, defined as the moment the nestling emerges from the calcareous egg, was recorded at approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days]. This incubation period aligns with values observed for other large-bodied Meliphagidae, though field studies suggest that natural nest temperatures can fluctuate considerably, extending the hatching window up to 16 days in cooler microclimates. The altricial nestling, which weighs only a few grams at emergence, begins its rapid growth trajectory under the constant attention of both parents. After hatching, the chick remains entirely dependent on parental provisioning and brooding, its body mass increasing exponentially as it consumes a diet rich in nectar and invertebrates. This initial stage is critical for establishing thermoregulatory capacity and immune competence before the more demanding fledging period commences.

Sexual size dimorphism is pronounced in the Tui, a characteristic that influences both foraging ecology and reproductive strategies. The ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum recorded adult body mass, reaches 89.6 grams [Wwi = 89.6 grams] for females and 124.9 grams [Wwi = 124.9 grams] for males, making males roughly one-third heavier than their counterparts. This disparity is thought to reflect sexual selection for larger male body size in contests over prime feeding territories, particularly around flowering nectar sources where competition is intense. At the same time, the smaller female body mass may allow for greater agility during nest construction and provisioning of the developing chick. Field measurements from museum specimen series confirm that these values are stable across populations, though local variation in food availability can lead to modest shifts in mean adult mass. Such differences in body size also carry implications for overall metabolic expenditure and longevity within the species.

Reproductive output in the Tui is relatively modest compared to other New Zealand passerines. Females lay between 2 and 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 2 and 4 eggs per clutch], with only a single clutch produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch produced each year], likely a constraint imposed by the prolonged period of parental care required by the altricial nestling. Under the thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic period for this species, measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the time since birth at fledging is 14.5 days [tx = 14.5 days], a remarkably short interval that belies the intense energetic demands placed on the parents during the nestling phase. After leaving the nest, the fledgling remains dependent on the adults for several additional weeks as it masters flight and learns to forage independently. The combination of a single annual clutch and a small clutch size makes the Tui vulnerable to predation pressure and habitat loss, which can severely impact population recruitment.

The life history of the Tui is characterized by a slow pace relative to its body size, with considerable investment in each reproductive event. Under the standard metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for this species is 13.5 years [am = 13.5 years], a longevity that exceeds that of many other passerines of comparable mass. Puberty, defined here as the onset of gonadal maturation, is reached at 44 days since birth [tp = 44 days since birth] under these same thermal conditions at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].
